summary: Let’s talk about this… Where do I even start? It seems like a lot of people are feeling this too. The constant barrage of new products, models, capabilities, threats, whatever is one thing. content: AI is overwhelming and I’m doing it wrong - Ben's Bites Subscribe Sign in AI is overwhelming and I’m doing it wrong Let’s think about what we’re doing here Oct 29, 2026 63 10 8 Share Let’s talk about this… Ben Tossell @ bentossell i feel stuck with wtf i do for like 10 months keep going round in circles. questioning and re-questioning everything. things feel exciting then dont. what feels like a good business direction then doesnt. touch grass, ai melting brains, i know i know but still 8:41 AM · Oct 28, 2026 · 82.5K Views 163 Replies · 9 Reposts · 681 Likes Where do I even start? It seems like a lot of people are feeling this too. The constant barrage of new products, models, capabilities, threats, whatever is one thing. But seeing people with 20 personal agents for managing their social content or just life. What are we doing here?! When I first started the newsletter it was to keep up with everything that was going on. It was 5 days a week. It was so noisy I decided to cut it down (along with our revenue) to just two days. I try and cut through the noise with the links here but the noise is still there, it may be louder. I read two excellent posts yesterday. Here’s a snippet from each You’re doing your best to keep up. You’re 9-9-6’ing, sometimes 0-0-7’ing. You didn’t actually rest during rest week, did you? What are your agents up to? Hopefully getting a lot done while you’re reading this. Have you tried the latest personal assistant? Optimized your workflows to accommodate the strengths of the latest model? Have you gone viral on X lately? Have you been angel investing? Have you locked in your Bay Area mortgage? If not, you know you’re fucked, right? You’re enslaved to your keyboard, timeline, and Slack. You’re tired, but your ambition is also Icarus-ing. Your FOMO is spiking. Your capacity is redlining. Is your moral compass spinning? The Sane Asylum by Colossus To be blunt, instead of having to sit down and “do” a thing, you can, while hungover in sweats on your couch, grab your laptop, fire up Claude Code, Codex, GrokBot, whatever, and just tell it to start building whatever epiphany is top of mind at the moment. Oh, and you don’t even have to type it anymore. Hands too sore? You can double tap the function key and your space bar, have Wispr Flow start transcribing, and say, “I want you to build a tool that each day goes through all newsletters I’m subscribed to, find the key highlights from each that I should care about, and send me a summary. Make this a daily routine, thanks.” Then go back to vegging out on your couch while your little token muncher cranks away. The Difference Between “Can” and “Should” by Jack Raines I start far more than I finish. I have a course that’s ~70% done, I have a tool for non-techies using personal agents that’s 80% done. content: Is Anthropic the best business in the world? - Ben's Bites Subscribe Sign in Is Anthropic the best business in the world? Lots of visuals to use and learn with. Oct 27, 2026 31 4 Share Hi folks, I’m still figuring things out, this newsletter, my videos, my style, everything is on the table. Today’s video is a bit of a behind the scenes of how I’m working through that and finding my style. It’s still a work in progress but lmk what you think. You can view the full session post here . Also linked there is my visual breakdown of Anthropic’s IPO filing. Share Ben's Bites My feed GPT-6.1 Terra is OpenAI’s new model for computer use and writing. Easy choice for a daily driver on the $20 plan. Half the price of Sol and very competent. It doesn’t make the dumb mistakes Luna often does. Stacklet Token Custodian - know which agent is burning your token budget, then act on it with automated policy across AI providers.* With your approval, 1Password for Agents can sign your agent into a site without revealing your password. It’s rolling out for Muse and Grok Bot. Kimi K3.1 Pro - a new open-source model. Benchmarks say it’s at Opus 5.5 level. Dessa - speech model from Block. It can listen and speak at the same time. I didn’t love it like others on X did… the first example feels like you’re talking to an annoying idiot. Sure it’s expressive and sounds like a human. Hallmark is a rebuilt design skill for agents, that refuses to look AI generated. What is an agent harness , anyway? Browserbase introduced BELL , an open-source personal assistant stack Grok Bot can use the calendar, reminders and contacts on your phone. Plus it has a 1Password integration and can save logins and cards. Thorsten Ball shares his agent workflow : describe outcomes, generate variations, request proof, and use scheduled checks rather than constant back-and-forth. Reduck lets agents use the web quickly and reliably (and get around websites that block agents…) pwn.watch tracks live security incidents that agents can monitor on a schedule. Coworkers - build your own AI teammates, each with a computer and browser, on Cloudflare. (experimental) A few illustration skills: Teardown - turn an object into an editable technical illustration you can export. D imensional drawings of UI components Michael is building Charming . It’s like Notion for tiny apps (vs docs). He made this to-do board template on it, inspired by my post last Tuesday. Subscribe Afters Techartist @ techartist_ Education doesn’t have to be text and flat diagrams. So I’m building a 3D book about energy that students can play with: 10 lessons to predict, test and prove. Built with Opus 5.5 and Three.js. summary: Hi folks, I’ve been working on a way to get my X bookmarks grouped in the right places for the newsletter. content: Claude’s personal agent - Ben's Bites Subscribe Sign in Claude’s personal agent And how I run the newsletter with agents Oct 22, 2026 46 4 1 Share Hi folks, I’ve been working on a way to get my X bookmarks grouped in the right places for the newsletter. If you didn’t know, Keshav , who’s been working with me for many years, is leaving us at the end of the year to dive further into the exciting world of AI. He used to do a lot of the work behind the scenes, getting our links ready. This is what I’ve built and am using as of this week. You can see the full write-up here . Share Ben's Bites Oh and one other change to Ben’s Bites - we’re changing how we work with sponsors…from 2027 we’re only going to work closely with 4 companies per quarter (a ‘season’) where I’ll be building with the tools, telling their story through sessions I share. I’ll only approve companies I admire, respect and want to use (or already do!) and they can’t sign off on what I can say. If you’re interested in applying, our new partner page is here . My feed Anthropic has entered the personal agent/assistant race with Duet . A separate app (mobile, US-only) in research preview, so I can’t use it 😭. I imagine it’ll be pretty good with rough edges, like the rest of them. Big security issues yesterday with PHP (a programming language that a lot of the internet runs on) and Railway (a hosting platform). I pinged Codex yesterday ‘check if any of my work uses PHP or Railway, assess any risks and address them.’ OpenAI helped researchers find these vulnerabilities. You’ve heard of ‘browser-use’, now there’s phone use that lets agents use real Android and iPhones. Ethan Mollick’s new book, Co-Existence , explores living and working with AI that is sometimes, but not always, better than people. Supermemory introduced a memory graph that extracts facts from documents, links related memories, and resolves updates while preserving previous versions. Grok Bot can build and update pages , with suggested uses including morning briefs, design documents, and weekly work summaries. Told ya. I still will use here.now because I want all my different agent apps to be able to use my pages (like my todo board). SF Compute CEO Evan Conrad discusses programmable data centers , GPU trading, and physical settlement on Latent Space. Dan Shipper argues companies should create a frontier team to track changing AI models and share what it learns with colleagues. Hey Keshav here. If you're a small company (10-50 people) that likes what Dan is saying but can't just hire a team for keeping up with the frontier - I want to talk with you. I already do it for Ben's Bites, and I can do it for your company. DM me on X / email me Anthropic reports that 17 of 211 Claude-designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins met its experimental binding criteria. AgentReady is an open specification for making products usable by AI agents, organised around finding information, reading it, and taking action. Resend Inboxes

title: <![CDATA[30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)]]>
summary: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite love...
content: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) - by Ethan Mollick One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts) My new book is out today... what happened since the last one Ethan Mollick Oct 20, 2026 750 130 60 Share My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. F

title: <![CDATA[The Dot and the Swarm]]>
summary: I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with...
content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,367 229 140 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Dots and Muse The number one app in the App Store right now is Meta’s Muse, a personal agent that promises to do work for you. OpenAI has now released a competitor tool, called dots. They aren’t alone: SpaceX’s Grok Bot, Instinct, and Gemini Spark all do similar things, more or less. All of these agents draw inspiration from a phenomenon you might remember from earlier this year, OpenClaw. content: The Overhang - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Overhang Using your deep knowledge, wide knowledge, taste, and agency Ethan Mollick Sep 18, 2026 947 118 102 Share We are still on an exponential curve of AI development. I try to put out a Substack post every couple weeks or so, yet, as the pace speeds up, that sometimes feels too slow. In the weeks since my last post, we had the apparent cracking of one of the most famous problems in math by an AI (accompanied by controversy) and widespread discussions about the risks posed by AI and what to do about it (also accompanied by controversy). I think these concerns, along with a mounting set of other worries, come down to the same problem I have with my posts: how slowly our very human systems and processes work to keep up with the pace of AI development. I don't think the people worried about this are wrong, but I also think a sole focus on future AIs, as important as that is, ignores the fact that AI, right now, is already incredibly capable. In fact, the new GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 are already enough for transformative impact in large sections of the economy and they can reliably do weeks worth of human work when properly guided and harnessed. A few fun examples of that: I had GPT-6 Astra turn a 1977 text adventure game called Zork into a full 3D action-adventure game you can play . Zork has no graphics and each location is a paragraph of prose, so the AI had to decide what the white house looks like, what a grue looks like (the original only tells you that you are likely to be eaten by one in the dark), and how to turn “fight the troll” into an action sequence. I also had Fable 5.1 try to reconstruct Italian author Umberto Eco’s library in 3D . Eco kept tens of thousands of books in his Milan apartment and the AI could not find a floor plan, so it instead decided to work from a dozen videos, the foundation's photographs of each bookcase, and two library catalogues. It read spines frame by frame, inferred the rooms, and placed the 5,000 or so books it could identify among 27,000 shelf slots. It marked every book certain, guess, or unknown, and drew the bookcases the cameras never reached in fog. This task, like the Zork game and a lot of real-world work I have had the AI do recently, would have taken weeks of human work involving researchers, coders, and designers. But here we are. My point is that, while there is a lot of debate over what future models will do, the current capabilities of existing models are barely being used, and are often not even well understood. For example, I did not know GPT-6 Astra could operate Blender (a sophisticated piece of 3D modelling software) until it did. I gave it a copy of my upcoming book, Co-Existence , and asked it to create a trailer for the book from the perspective of an AI. summary: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and GitLab, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. content: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks? Subscribe Sign in Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks? Nathan Lambert Oct 30, 2026 38 11 6 Share Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and GitLab, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. Share Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache.
